screening_decisions.reason: Randomised controlled trial in women with stress USI. One arm received PFMT (pelvic floor exercises via digital palpation or biofeedback); the third arm was an untreated control group. Meets all criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in women with SUI. The intervention was a mobile app that guided PFMT (98% performed PFMT), and the control group was postponed treatment (i.e. no active treatment during the trial).

Randomised controlled trial in postmenopausal women with stress UI. Three arms: PFME alone, PFME with biofeedback, and a control group that received no exercise treatment. Both PFME arms are PFMT, and a no‑treatment control is present.

Randomised placebo‑controlled trial in women with urge or urge‑predominant mixed UI. One arm was biofeedback‑assisted behavioural treatment, which typically includes PFMT; another arm was a placebo control. The PFMT component is not described in detail but behavioural treatment for urge incontinence frequently incorporates pelvic floor exercises.
Randomised controlled trial in women with stress incontinence. Arms: biofeedback, pelvic muscle exercise (both PFMT), and a control group that received no exercise. All criteria satisfied.

Multicentre, single‑blind randomised controlled trial in women with urodynamically proven genuine stress incontinence. Arms: pelvic floor exercises (PFMT) and an untreated control group. Meets criteria.

Experimental study with random assignment of women with SUI. The experimental group underwent 16 sessions of pelvic floor exercises; the control group received no such treatment. Satisfies the criteria.
Single‑blind randomised controlled trial in women with urodynamic stress UI. One arm was pelvic floor exercises (PFMT); another was an untreated control. All criteria met.

Prospective randomised controlled trial in women with stress and mixed UI. The PFMT group performed a 12‑week home‑based exercise programme; the control group received no such intervention. Meets criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in women with UI. The treatment group received a behavioural modification programme that included pelvic floor muscle training; the control group had no treatment. Despite UI type not being classified as SUI/UUI/MUI, the trial assessed cough stress test, suggesting stress incontinence is included.

Prospective randomised study comparing medical gymnastics (likely PFMT) with electrical stimulation, but no untreated or inactive control group is mentioned in the abstract. Does not meet the requirement of a no‑treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm.

Randomised, controlled, crossover trial in elderly women with stress UI. The intervention group received pelvic floor and fitness exercises for 3 months; the control group (parallel phase) received no exercise and served as an inactive comparator. Satisfies criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in women aged ≥ 70 with stress, urge and mixed UI. The exercise‑only group performed PFMT and was compared with an education group that did not receive exercise. The education arm acted as an inactive control.

Randomised controlled trial in community‑dwelling Japanese women with stress, urge and mixed UI. The intervention group received multidimensional exercises including PFMT; the control group received no intervention and showed no improvement.

Randomised controlled trial in older Chinese women with stress, urge or mixed UI. The intervention group received a structured continence physiotherapy programme (including PFMT with manual feedback); the control group received only advice and an educational pamphlet (an inactive control). Meets criteria.
Randomised controlled trial in women with SUI. The treatment group received 12 weekly physiotherapist‑supervised PFMT sessions; the control group received no treatment. Satisfies all criteria.

Randomised, single‑blind trial in women with mild‑to‑moderate SUI. Women taught the “Knack” (a timed pelvic floor contraction) were compared with a wait‑list control that had not yet been taught. PFMT arm vs. no‑treatment control.

Randomised controlled pilot study in women with SUI. Arms: PFMT in group treatment, PFMT in individual treatment, and a control group that received no treatment during the corresponding period. Meets criteria.
Pilot randomised trial in women with mixed urinary incontinence. One arm was PFMT; another was a waiting list control (no active treatment). Satisfies criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in postmenopausal women with UI (type not specified, but included 7‑day bladder diary episodes). The physical therapy arm included PFMT for UI; the control group received osteoporosis education (an inactive control).

Randomised trial comparing bladder training, pelvic muscle exercise (PFMT), and a control group. The abstract states the two intervention groups improved compared with the control group, indicating a no‑treatment control. UI type not specified but the pelvic muscle exercise group is PFMT.

Experimental study with random assignment of women with stress UI. Groups: electrical stimulation plus kinesitherapy, kinesitherapy alone (PFMT), and a control group. The PFMT arm and a no‑treatment control are present.

Randomised trial in female volleyball athletes with stress urinary incontinence. The experimental group received a pelvic floor muscle rehabilitation programme; the control group received only a pamphlet (inactive control).
Randomised trial in women with genuine stress incontinence. The pelvic floor exercises group (PFMT) was compared with other non‑operative treatments and an untreated control group. Meets criteria.

Controlled trial (random assignment) in women with genuine stress incontinence in general practice. The treatment group received pelvic floor exercise instruction; the control group received no therapy. Satisfies criteria.
Parallel‑group randomised clinical trial in women with stress or mixed UI. The PFM training group performed exercises; the control group was untreated. All criteria satisfied.
This paper describes a study protocol (the PromoCon trial). It is not a completed randomised controlled trial and therefore does not provide outcome data for screening.

This study assessed patient and GP satisfaction with nurse‑specialist‑led care versus usual GP care for UI. It does not evaluate a PFMT intervention against an inactive control; the comparison is between two active care models.

Randomised trial in women with urge UI. The three arms were biofeedback‑assisted behavioural training, behavioural training with verbal feedback, and a self‑help booklet. The booklet arm constituted an active (self‑administered) treatment, not a no‑treatment, placebo, sham or inactive control. Therefore the inactive‑control requirement is not met.
This is a feasibility study, not a randomised controlled trial. Participants volunteered and were not randomly assigned, so it does not meet the study design criterion.
Randomised trial comparing intensive supervised PFMT with unsupervised PFMT in women with SUI. Both arms received active PFMT; there is no no‑treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm.
Randomised trial in women with low back pain and stress UI. The control group received routine physiotherapy (active treatment); there is no inactive control arm.

Randomised trial in women with stress or stress‑predominant mixed UI. The control group was a self‑administered behavioral treatment using a self‑help booklet, which is an active intervention, not an inactive control.

Randomised controlled trial in elderly women with UI residing in long‑term care. The training group received a program including Kegel’s exercises (PFMT); the control group received no structured exercise program. Meets criteria.
Randomised controlled trial in women with UI in India. The intervention group received behavioral therapy (which included PFMT); the control group received no therapy. Controls were inactive.

Economic evaluation alongside an RCT comparing internet‑based PFMT with a postal PFMT programme. The trial itself did not include a no‑treatment or inactive control arm; the economic comparison with no treatment was modelled, not randomised.

Randomised trial comparing internet‑based PFMT with a postal PFMT programme in women with SUI. Both arms are active PFMT interventions; there is no no‑treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm.
Long‑term follow‑up of the same trial as study 37. No inactive control arm was included in the original randomisation.

Randomised controlled trial in middle‑aged women with SUI. The exercise group performed co‑contraction of transverse abdominis and PFM; the control group received no such exercise. Small sample but meets criteria.

Pilot randomised controlled trial in frail older women with UI. The intervention combined behavioral UI treatments (which include PFMT) with physical activity; the control group received no active treatment. Meets criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in gynecological cancer survivors with pelvic floor dysfunction. The population is not specifically defined as having SUI, UUI, or MUI; pelvic floor dysfunction may include other symptoms beyond UI.
This is a study describing the development and psychometric testing of the ICIQ questionnaire. It is not a randomised or quasi‑randomised controlled trial.
This is a systematic review of randomised clinical trials, not a primary trial. It does not meet the study design criterion.
This is a systematic review of randomised clinical trials, not a primary trial.
This paper is an explanation and elaboration of the CONSORT extension for non‑pharmacologic treatments. It is not a trial.
This is a general review‑style article on the impact of incontinence on self‑efficacy and quality of life. Not a randomised or quasi‑randomised controlled trial.
This is a psychometric study evaluating cross‑cultural performance of the I‑QOL measure. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This study focuses on the reproducibility of instruments to measure subjective evaluation of SUI. It is not a trial of an intervention.
This is an observational study using dynamic MRI to assess pelvic floor function in continent and incontinent women. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a discussion/review article about theories on why PFMT works for SUI. It is not a primary trial.
This is a joint terminology report by IUGA/ICS. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a cross‑sectional internet survey (secondary analysis of the EpiLUTS study). Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a book chapter reviewing the pharmacology of the lower urinary tract. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a review article discussing optimal PFMT regimens. It is not a primary randomised controlled trial.
This is a short descriptive paper on bladder inhibition with functional electrical stimulation. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a secondary analysis of pelvic muscle resting responses to exercise. Not a randomised controlled trial of PFMT vs. inactive control.
This is a GRADE guideline article. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a GRADE guideline article. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a community‑based epidemiological survey (the Norwegian EPINCONT study). It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a joint terminology report (IUGA/ICS). Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a methodological article about assessing quality of interventions in systematic reviews. Not a primary trial.
This is a cross‑sectional study using the Sickness Impact Profile in women with UI. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a systematic review and economic modelling study. It is not a primary randomised controlled trial.
This is the development and psychometric testing paper for the Bristol Female Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms questionnaire. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a willingness‑to‑pay study among incontinence patients. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a cross‑sectional analysis of the association between UI and self‑rated health. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This describes the development and validation of a condition‑specific quality‑of‑life questionnaire. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This paper reports the development of the York Incontinence Perceptions Scale. While it involved a longitudinal randomized control study, the paper itself is an instrument development study.
This is a content‑validity study of the King’s Health Questionnaire in overactive bladder patients. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a meta‑epidemiological study examining the effect of trial quality on meta‑analysis results. Not a primary randomised controlled trial.
This is the revised CONSORT statement paper. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a cross‑sectional survey assessing bothersomeness and quality of life impact of UI. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is an observational study of pelvic muscle activity in nulliparous women. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This paper compares a severity index with pad‑weighing tests. It is not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a cross‑sectional study examining the impact of UI on female sexual function. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a responsiveness and clinical utility study of the Geriatric Self‑Efficacy Index. It is not a randomised controlled trial evaluating PFMT vs. inactive control.
This paper describes short forms of the IIQ and UDI. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is the development paper for the I‑QOL measure. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This study validates the Norwegian version of the Quality of Life Scale in psoriasis patients, not in urinary incontinence. Not a trial.
This is a validation study of two global impression questionnaires for incontinence. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is the original HADS scale paper. Not a randomised controlled trial of PFMT.

Randomised controlled trial in perimenopausal overweight women with stress incontinence. The intervention group received regular PFM exercises; the control group received no exercise. Satisfies criteria.

Randomised study (longitudinal experimental design) in women with stress UI. Three arms: electrotherapy + exercises, exercises alone (PFMT), and a control group. The PFMT arm and a no‑treatment control are present.
Randomised sham‑controlled trial in women with urodynamic stress incontinence, but the intervention was acupressure, not pelvic floor muscle training. Does not meet the PFMT arm criterion.

Randomised trial comparing supervised pelvic floor exercise program with a conventional home prescribed exercise program in women with SUI. Both arms involve active PFMT; there is no inactive control arm.

Randomised, blinded, doubly controlled trial in women with SUI. Arms included PFMT alone, duloxetine alone, combined, and a no active treatment arm (imitation PFMT + placebo). The PFMT‑alone arm vs. the no active treatment arm satisfies the criteria.
This is a qualitative interview study exploring women’s experiences of two PFMT delivery programmes. It does not report a randomised controlled trial outcome.
This is a secondary analysis of predictors of success from a non‑face‑to‑face PFMT programme. It is not itself a randomised controlled trial with separate arms.
This is a Cochrane systematic review. Not a primary randomised controlled trial.
This is a review article on PFM exercise from an exercise physiology perspective. Not a primary randomised controlled trial.
This is a descriptive anatomical article. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This paper describes the Hopkins Symptom Checklist. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is a book chapter on adult conservative management. Not a primary randomised controlled trial.
This is a methodological article on post‑randomisation exclusions. Not a primary trial.
This is a Cochrane systematic review. Not a primary randomised controlled trial.
This is a review of outcome measures for lower urinary tract dysfunction studies. Not a randomised controlled trial.
This is an observational cohort study nested within a quasi‑experimental study. It is not itself a randomised controlled trial.

Randomised trial comparing urodynamic investigations prior to conservative treatment versus no urodynamics. Both groups received active conservative treatment (physiotherapy and bladder retraining); there is no PFMT vs. inactive control comparison.
This is a clinical and physiologic study of the pathophysiology of incontinence in institutionalized elderly. It is not a randomised controlled trial of an intervention.
This is a Cochrane systematic review on PFMT for prevention and treatment of incontinence in antenatal and postnatal women. Not a primary randomised controlled trial.
